passage:
At pickup time in the preschool corridor, Dhruv ran to his father, Manoj, with his shoes untied. "Papa, it fell again and Ma'am put it back and then it was okay!"
"What fell?"
"It! The one near the window!" Dhruv frowned, puzzled that Papa didn't know. "And Chirag was sad, so I'm sad, and you're sad too, na?"
Manoj knelt. "I wasn't there, beta. Show me the window."
Dhruv tugged him to the classroom door and pointed at a pot of mint on the sill, soil still scattered.

qa.q: What had fallen near the window?
qa.a: A pot of mint on the sill.

qa.q: Why does Dhruv look puzzled when Papa asks what fell?
qa.a: Dhruv saw it fall, so it seems obvious to him; he assumes his father already knows what he knows, and the question feels strange 🤔

qa.q: What choice helped Manoj make sense of the half-story?
qa.a: Manoj knelt, said he hadn't been there, and asked Dhruv to show him, turning a puzzling story into something he could see.

qa.q: What is it like for Manoj to hear 'it fell again' with no idea what 'it' is?
qa.a: Manoj is left guessing and can tell Dhruv expects him to know, so he has to stay patient and find another way in.

grounding: A preschooler tells his father a half-story as if he had been there and assumes everyone shares his sad feeling.

passage:
My brother Kunal is five, and his school stories come in pieces. Last night at dinner he said, "Then Miss said no, and the orange one was mine."
Mummy asked, "Which orange one?"
He sighed like she was being slow. "THE orange one."
After dinner he made Mummy a birthday card with a dinosaur sticker on it. Dinosaurs are his favourite thing in the world, so maybe he thought they'd be hers too. I can't really tell what goes on in his head. But Mummy put the dinosaur card on the fridge.
— Bhavna

qa.q: What sticker did Kunal put on Mummy's birthday card?
qa.a: A dinosaur sticker.

qa.q: Why did Kunal sigh when Mummy asked which orange one?
qa.a: Kunal feels impatient because the orange one is so clear in his own mind that he seems to think Mummy must already know it, so her question seems slow.

qa.q: What could Mummy ask next time to get the whole school story from Kunal?
qa.a: She could ask small questions one at a time, like where he was and who was with him, so Kunal can fill in what she didn't see.

qa.q: How might Mummy feel about getting a dinosaur card for her birthday?
qa.a: Mummy is likely amused and touched, since Kunal picked his own favourite thing for her, and she shows it by putting the card on the fridge ❤️

grounding: An older sibling watches a five-year-old tell half-stories and choose a gift from his own tastes, assuming others know and want what he does.

passage:
Monday. Joseph, four, climbed into the car and said, "The big one fell down and everybody went ooh!"
Anjali, his mother, asked, "What big one?"
He looked at her as if she had been there. "The BIG one, Amma."
Wednesday. At the school gate she tried a new question. "Tell me like I was at home all day."
Joseph thought hard. "The block tower. Ravi made it. It fell."
Next Monday. Before she could ask, he said, "You weren't there, so I'll tell you from the start."

qa.q: Who made the block tower?
qa.a: Ravi made it.

qa.q: Why did Joseph look at Anjali as if she had been there?
qa.a: Joseph was so excited about the tower falling that he assumed his mother saw it too, so 'the big one' seemed like enough explanation.

qa.q: Which question on Wednesday changed how Joseph told his story?
qa.a: Asking him to tell it 'like I was at home all day' reminded Joseph that his mother hadn't seen it, and he began naming things.

qa.q: What is it like for Anjali in the car on Monday?
qa.a: Anjali is left puzzling over 'the big one' and can tell Joseph expects her to know, so she has to hunt for the story without making him feel silly.

grounding: Over a week, a four-year-old who assumed his mother saw his day starts to tell his story from the beginning.

passage: Rain was pouring and the auto meter was ticking outside the preschool gate when Nikita reached Gautam, four. He grabbed her hand. "Mummy, the big one fell and Riya cried and Ma'am got the thing!" "Which big one? What thing?" she asked, fighting with the umbrella. Gautam frowned, as if she were being silly. "The one! You know!" In the auto he pressed his face to the window. "You're sad too, because the swings are wet," he said. Nikita, who had not thought about swings all day, squeezed his hand. "Tell me slowly. What fell first?"

qa.q: Who cried, according to Gautam?
qa.a: Riya.

qa.q: Why did Gautam frown when Nikita asked "Which big one?"
qa.a: He assumed she already knew what he had seen at school, so her question seemed silly to him.

qa.q: What did Nikita try, and why does it suit a four-year-old?
qa.a: She asked him to tell it slowly and start with what fell first, which helps him fill in the story step by step.

qa.q: What is it like for Nikita trying to follow the story in the rain?
qa.a: It's confusing and a bit stressful, with the meter ticking and the umbrella fighting her, yet she stays patient.

grounding: A preschool boy tells his mother a half-story assuming she knows what he saw, and assumes she shares his feelings about the swings.

passage: In their Pune flat, Yuvraj, five, burst in from school. "Mummy, Bittu did it again and then the fish!" Sharmila put down her tea. "Who's Bittu? What fish?" Yuvraj stamped his foot. "Bittu, Mummy! You know!" His Minakshi Masi, visiting, tried: "Was the fish in a tank?" "Obviously." Then he held out his chocolate to Masi. "You want it. Everybody loves orange ones." Masi, who disliked orange chocolates, took a tiny bite and smiled. Sharmila sat down beside him. "Start from the bus. What happened first?"

qa.q: What flavour of chocolate did Yuvraj offer Masi?
qa.a: An orange one.

qa.q: Why did Yuvraj stamp his foot when Sharmila asked who Bittu was?
qa.a: He believed his mother already knew Bittu and the fish, so her question felt frustrating to him.

qa.q: What small step did Sharmila take to help Yuvraj tell the story?
qa.a: She sat beside him and asked him to start from the bus, giving him a simple order to follow.

qa.q: How might Minakshi Masi feel about the orange chocolate?
qa.a: Masi doesn't like orange ones but took a tiny bite to be kind, seeing that Yuvraj assumed everyone shares his taste.

grounding: A preschool boy gives puzzling half-stories, assuming his mother knows what he saw, and thinks everyone likes what he likes.
